sections.section: Dartvel — The Complete Vision, to be implemented

sections.absent: Nothing named. Both @DVBackendCron and @DVClientCron are collected into generated entries and DVScheduler runs them: the note that client cron generation was missing was wrong, and what was actually missing was any cron evaluator at all -- the schedule travelled from an annotation into a generated list and stopped there
nothing. Seven adapters -- in-memory, database, Redis, SQS, RabbitMQ, Pub/Sub and Kafka -- and the four network ones are verified against a real broker in CI rather than against a fake
Biometric sign-in, which is a device capability rather than a server one and is tracked under Platform bindings. LDAP, SAML, passkey and Web3 ship.

Per-platform native bindings remain unbound where the capability has no host API to reach: measured now rather than estimated, that is 28 names on Linux (bound since: deepLinks.initial, a desktop deep link being a launch argument; media.pick, the file chooser with the kind's filters; permissions.isGranted and request, which say what a desktop grants without asking and answer false where a system service Dartvel has no binding for would have to be asked), 24 on web, and on Windows and macOS fewer since kiosk enforcement, global shortcuts, the application menu, the tray, the device APIs and display enumeration were bound (kiosk on the web too), and 30 on iOS, many of which are not applicable to the platform at all (NFC and haptics on a desktop). files.readBytes/writeBytes/delete now ship for every platform with a filesystem.. DV.Platform.screen is now also reachable reactively as context.screen, which reads MediaQuery and so rebuilds on a resize; the plain getters read the raw window and register no dependency, so a widget built on them laid out once at first-frame size and never reflowed. The generated runtime now registers the running platform's bindings itself; until it did, no generated application called DVLinuxBindings.register() or its siblings, and every platform API on desktop threw "binding not registered" in a real app while the matrix reported the bindings as implemented

nothing. SQLite, PostgreSQL and MySQL, each with their wire-compatible variants, and TLS on both network engines so managed endpoints are reachable. MongoDB, ClickHouse and BigQuery are out of scope by decision, not backlog

no provider has been exercised against a real APNS or push service; the native transport they depend on speaks HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 and is verified live, and the VAPID signature is now pinned byte-for-byte to RFC 6979's published P-256 vectors rather than only round-tripped through this library's own verifier -- but a signature a push service would accept is not the same as a request one has accepted

Nothing this section lists is unbuilt. Background sync is exercised in a real browser: the generated worker keeps an IndexedDB outbox of same-origin non-GET requests that could not be sent, answers the caller with a 202 and X-Dartvel-Queued, and replays the outbox in order when the network is back, stopping at the first failure and one replay at a time (a sync event and the client's replay message arriving together sent everything twice until they shared one in-flight promise). dartvel capture pwa-sync loads the built worker in Chrome, takes the server away, makes a POST, brings the server back and expects the POST to arrive; the Runtime verification workflow runs it against the site's own build on every push, and it is what found the double replay. Everything else the section lists is built: manifest, viewport, service worker, offline page, install prompt, and icon generation from web/icon.png through the CLI's own PNG codec
Shorebird-backed native patch application; page bundles ship as data and do not need it

Profiling and performance analysis. Logs, metrics, traces and error reporting are built: DVMetrics renders Prometheus text exposition and GET /metrics serves it, DVHealth backs GET /health with real checks on a deadline, and tracing carries W3C Trace Context across the request boundary with sampling decided from the trace id alone -- a per-process decision samples a four-service request with probability p^4, which reads as tracing being on and finding nothing

Nothing named. Generated factories now carry a sequence, so two create() calls produce two records rather than one repeated identifier, with createMany for list-shaped tests and resetSequence so a snapshot assertion is repeatable. Every test mode resolves, and a mode with no tests reports that it has none and where it looked

Algolia is exercised only against a recorded transport: it is a hosted service with no local server, so its request shape is pinned by unit tests rather than by a round trip. Meilisearch and OpenSearch are verified live in CI.

App-store and Play Billing purchases, which need the store bindings. Stripe and Paddle are built: checkout for a plan's configured price, and webhooks that grant and revoke entitlements from subscription status -- each believed only when its own signature scheme matches in constant time within five minutes (Stripe's t=/v1= over 't.payload', Paddle's ts=/h1= over 'ts:payload', and each provider refuses the other's), with the key never echoed in an error and a sandbox Paddle key routed to the sandbox host by the key itself. Not exercised against either service; the tests inject the HTTP and the clock

Nothing this section asks for is unbuilt. Switch control and hardware-key navigation are built: DVSwitchControl steps focus through a page with one key and activates with another, wrapping, with auto-scan for a single-switch user; DVHardwareKeys maps a remote's D-pad and select onto focus and activation; DVAccessibilityToggle is the attract-route toggle behind DV.Accessibility.switchControl; DVAccessibilityKeys.isExempt names the keys a kiosk hardware-key block must let through, which is the rule Kiosk Mode's native enforcement consults when it exists (that enforcement is Kiosk Mode's gap, not this section's). Waivers are built: dartvel.accessibility.waivers names a route, a rule the audit has (or * for the page) and a reason -- no reason, no waiver -- and a waiver that matches nothing is reported so it does not sit in the file for ever. The release gate is built: dartvel build web audits the semantics tree a real browser produced -- what a screen reader is actually handed -- and fails on a link or control with no accessible name, an empty heading, a page with no headings or no level 1, and a heading level skipped going down; on its first run against the site it found /features going h1 to h3. Generated tables have keyboard navigation, focus that survives a sort, and per-cell announcements naming the column and the row position. Contrast is checked against WCAG ratios and tap targets against Material's minimum

Drag and drop is built: a window accepts drops of the kinds it says it takes -- files, text, or both -- and each drop arrives as what was dropped and where, an empty drop or one after stop reaching nobody; on Linux the toplevel becomes a GTK drop target whose drag-data-received payload is read by its type, so one path serves a file manager's uri-list and a browser's text, and what GTK already took is kept and given back on stop. The uri-list is parsed as RFC 2483 has it, percent escapes decoded and a URI that is not a file left out. Exercised under Xvfb against real GTK, with a real GtkSelectionData built through the clipboard and the signal emitted the way a drop emits it. The tray is built on Linux, as the protocol has it rather than as a picture: a StatusNotifierItem and its com.canonical.dbusmenu menu are exported on the session bus and registered with the shell's StatusNotifierWatcher, which is how a modern desktop is told about a tray icon -- no XEmbed, nothing deprecated, no GTK. The suite stands up a watcher of its own the way a shell would, reads the item's title, icon, status, category and menu path back over the bus, walks the menu layout, sends an Event the way a click arrives and sees it reach the application by id, and watches the name leave the bus on hide. What a runner cannot check is the pixels, and nothing claims them: a desktop with no watcher leaves the item exported and says so. Drag and drop is built on all three desktops. On Windows it is an OLE drop target: a COM object with a vtable of seven functions, registered with RegisterDragDrop, reading CF_HDROP for the files a file manager drags and CF_UNICODETEXT for a browser's text, with the POINTL each method takes declared as the eight bytes it travels in rather than as a struct by value in a callback; the live suite gives it a real IDataObject -- the clipboard's, which is the same interface Explorer hands over, carrying a DROPFILES built the way a file manager builds one -- and calls Drop the way OLE calls it. On macOS the window's content view is registered as a dragging destination and the two dragging methods are added to its class at runtime, reading the whole file list a file manager writes rather than the first of it; the live suite checks that reading against a real pasteboard, files and text, and that a process with no window is refused and says so. What a runner cannot do is drag from another application: on both, the drag is not claimed and everything the drop does is. Absent: on Windows and macOS the file associations' registration at run time; the launch handover is now exercised on both, since the single-instance lock's two-process suite runs on those runners as well as on Linux. The device and fleet APIs are built on Linux: the capability manifest (a provisioned or generated-and-kept id; cores, memory, kernel, display, touch, and the bindings actually registered rather than the names declared), health as a verdict with uptime, load, memory, disk and temperature behind it from procfs and sysfs, a watchdog that restarts on a missed heartbeat and tells systemd through sd_notify so WatchdogSec= works, restart-loop detection reported as DV-KIOSK-008 instead of restarting again, provisioning kept across starts, and a diagnostics bundle. File associations and app links are built on Linux: dartvel build linux writes the desktop entry (Exec with %U, MimeType for every association and x-scheme-handler for every scheme) and shared-mime-info XML for the types the app introduces from dartvel.desktop in pubspec.yaml, and the generated runtime opens what the app was launched with -- DVAppLaunch takes the single-instance lock, maps each argument to a route without trusting it as one, opens it as an external window request, and a later launch hands its arguments to the first and ends. Printing is built on Linux: DV.Platform.Printing draws pictures onto pages through GtkPrintOperation, to a PDF with no dialog (verified under Xvfb, poppler reading the page count back) or through the print dialog. System dialogs are built on Linux: DV.Platform.Dialogs opens, saves, chooses a folder and shows a message through GTK, verified under Xvfb by a seam that answers the dialog from GTK's own loop the way a person would. Built on Linux and tested under Xvfb: global shortcuts, grabbed through XGrabKey on a pump isolate's own X connection with XTest pressing the keys in the test; and the application menu, built as a real GtkMenuBar into the toplevel window with the view reparented beneath it, read back through GTK and activated by id. Both have the Dart side everywhere -- DVAccelerator parsed once, DVShortcuts and DVMenus delivering by id. Built since on Windows and macOS, each exercised on its own runner by the live suite: global shortcuts (RegisterHotKey on a pump thread of its own that delivers WM_HOTKEY by id, proven by posting the message Win32 sends and by a synthesised press where the session takes input; Carbon's RegisterEventHotKey with one handler dispatching by id, registration and the refusal of a duplicate proven, delivery said to need the application's event loop); the application menu (a Win32 menu bar on the process's window, subclassed so WM_COMMAND is dispatched by id, proven on a window the test owns; NSMenu as NSApp's main menu with every item targeting one runtime-defined Objective-C object, read back and activated through AppKit); the tray icon with its menu delivered by id (Shell_NotifyIcon on the process's window, refused where the session has no notification area; an NSStatusBar item sharing the menu's target under a second action) -- the Dart side of the tray now delivers a chosen item to onSelected and the selected stream; and the device APIs, the shared runtime reading through Win32 and through sysctl, Mach and getloadavg, real numbers from each runner. Multi-window and window state persistence are recorded under Multi-Window Startup is measured: the framework marks the phases it goes through -- configure, the generated registrations, the platform bindings, and the first frame, measured after the frame because a router that is built is not a screen that is up -- from one monotonic clock, and the report is the same shape every run, so two runs of the same build are comparable line by line and a budget names the phase that went over. The running application publishes it beside its live window list and the diagnostics bundle carries it, so a fleet asking why a device is slow to come up has the answer without sending anybody to the device; CI reads it back from the Linux run. Still absent from this section's embedded list: serial, USB, Bluetooth and NFC device APIs, boot-to-app packaging, and update channels for kiosk and device fleets.

The policy, the state machine and the enforcement matrix are built and validated by dartvel doctor, which fails a build configuration whose policy cannot be honoured. The session clock is built: the runtime notices idle, counts down for the warning span on a signal the countdown route reads, and at the timeout resets -- clearing what clearOnReset names through the app's clear callback and telling it to go home -- or only goes home, or nothing, as onIdle says; staff mode has no clock; a clear that fails leaves the kiosk failed. Hardware-key blocking is built on Linux: DVKiosk.enforce grabs every combo that leaves a kiosk through X11, riding the global-shortcut pump, filtered through the accessibility exemption so a kiosk blocks escape and never access, and reports what was held and what the server refused; verified under Xvfb with XTest, where Alt+Tab is swallowed and Tab is not. Fullscreen is asked of the GTK window when there is one. Declared policies parse with their refusals enforced -- a literal exit PIN, `auth` in a display-scope clearOnReset, an idle warning longer than the timeout. Exit attempts count to maxAttempts and lock out for lockoutFor, refusing even the right PIN while locked, and the lockout survives resume(). Enforcement resolves the specification's per-target strengths and reports DV-KIOSK-001, 002, 004 and 010; the runtime reports 003 and 005. The screen-side half is built: DVKioskHost turns any pointer or key into activity, shows the countdown while the runtime warns, sends the app home on a reset, and replaces the page with a diagnostics screen when the watchdog reports a restart loop -- which the Linux device binding does, counting startup arms and reporting the fourth in five minutes as DV-KIOSK-008 (restart-loop detection is therefore built); the watchdog itself restarts on a missed heartbeat and heartbeats systemd through sd_notify, which is what restart supervision under a systemd unit needs. Pointer confinement on Linux is built: DVKiosk.enforce holds the pointer inside the toplevel with a grab on the application's own X connection, verified under Xvfb with XTest warping the pointer outside and finding it inside. Notification suppression on Linux is built: the freedesktop notification the binding sends is held back while the kiosk holds, counted, and let through on release; the in-app inbox is not that binding and continues. System-gesture blocking is not applicable on an X11 desktop, which has no edge gestures to block. Kiosk windows in display scope are built under Multi-Window: DVWindowKind.kiosk, win.kiosk with state, enforcement, resetSession and exit, capability.displayKiosk. DV.Platform.display.kiosk is built: the generated runtime installs the declaration's device-scope policy at start, and the application observes the kiosk's state, reads what this platform honours, resets the session and leaves only through the declared exit method, the platform holding the policy on resume and letting go on exit. Native enforcement is built on the three desktops: Linux (XGrabKey, XGrabPointer, notification suppression), Windows (RegisterHotKey for the escape combos with the secure attention sequence and reserved keys reported unenforced, ClipCursor for the pointer, the window style for fullscreen; notifications never claimed) and macOS (NSApplication's presentation options, one fixed consistent set; a combo reported blocked only because the option covering it is in effect, Cmd+Q unenforced, pointer and notifications not claimed), each exercised on its own runner by the live suite; and on the web (Fullscreen, Keyboard Lock and Pointer Lock, each needing a user gesture and reported refused with the browser's reason when it is absent, a dedicated browser kiosk mode reported through the fullscreen display mode), exercised in Chrome by the browser suite. Absent: native enforcement on Android, iPadOS, Tizen, webOS and eLinux (DV-KIOSK-007 there). Built since: DVWindowKind.kiosk (display-scope kiosk windows, DV-WINDOW-010/011/012); deviceProfiles.<profile>.kiosk goes over the section in the generated DVKioskPolicies.device when dartvel build --device-profile selects that profile; dartvel inspect kiosk [--json] [--device-profile] prints the effective policy per target and per kiosk window with the source of each value (section, profile:<id>, policy:<name>, default). DVKioskPolicies.<name> is generated into the client's config from dartvel.kiosk.policies, each the section's settings with the named entry's over them; DV.lifecycle.kiosk is a read-only lifecycle signal the runtime drives and the kiosk host mirrors, so a reset shows as resetting -> active. DV-KIOSK-009 is built: dartvel doctor warns when onIdle: home has a model with a sensitive field in reach of an allowed route, naming both.

The terminal backend itself and the dartvel_cli_flt fork: rendering through the Kitty protocol with an ANSI fallback, and a distributable runner. Built: terminal size as a signal (DV.Platform.terminal.size, read from the attached terminal and again on SIGWINCH), and launch negotiation wired into the generated main -- a GUI-only build links no decision, a build with the terminal linked resolves from the arguments and the display, asks with the spec's wording when there is no display, and hands a terminal outcome to the runner beside the GUI binary

The performance contract is built: open() to ready (real and virtual), tear-out handover, shared-store write rate and coalescing ratio, store size and spill count, and restore-on-launch duration are measured; a call site that always degrades, a key written twice within a frame, a restore over the startup budget and owned windows outliving the frame budget on close are findings, one per subject; the running application publishes them beside its live window list and dartvel analyze performance aggregates degradations per call site, worst first. Built and tested: the generated runtime takes the single-instance lock at start, opens the arguments the process was launched with as external requests, hands a later launch's arguments to the first process and ends the later one (DVAppLaunch, wired through createDartvelRouter(arguments:) and the project template's main); window identity as canonical URL with idempotent open(), the window.open binding on Linux through dartvel_windowing (which is what flips capability.multiWindow), XRandR/Xinerama display enumeration behind window.displays, DVDisplayHint resolution that never falls back to another display, DV.Window.main with promotion, the exit policy (lastWindow/mainWindow/explicit, owned windows excluded), owned windows closing in reverse order with a closed owner refused rather than reparented, modality that degrades honestly where the OS cannot enforce it, the single-instance lock and external open requests draining into the running application, workspace restore dropping routes that no longer resolve, the reserved dv./workspace. shared-store namespaces, DV.Test.fakeWindowing, dartvel inspect windows, and the DV-WINDOW/DV-KIOSK registry behind dartvel explain, checked against this specification's own tables. Every code in the registry has an emitter: 001-013, with 006 the one error, raised when the claimed binding is missing or throws rather than filed under the OS declining (004). The live window list is built: the primary instance publishes what it has open beside its lock on every change, and `dartvel inspect windows` reads it while it is fresh and otherwise says the app is not running and when it was last seen. The Studio window inspector is built: a Windows tab in free Studio lists the window manager's windows live, each with a close. Kiosk windows are built: DVWindowKind.kiosk with a declared policy owns its display (another window asking for it is placed elsewhere, DV-WINDOW-011), is pinned (a close is refused, DV-WINDOW-012, until kiosk.exit satisfies the declared method), presents in place with its policy running when the display is gone or the host cannot pin (DV-WINDOW-010), and has a session of its own; capability.displayKiosk reports whether the host can pin. Still Designed: tear-out. Display enumeration is Linux-only: no other platform registers window.displays, so elsewhere it falls back to PlatformDispatcher.displays, which reports no panel name, no primary flag and no layout origin, and DVDisplayHint.primary and .secondary both resolve to null there. Device profile display names are carried into the generated client: dartvel build --device-profile becomes the DARTVEL_DEVICE_PROFILE define, DVDeviceProfiles carries every profile's display names, and the runtime installs the selected profile's before any window opens.

The entry here used to be a copy of Multi-Window's and described the wrong section. Built: the tab strip, reorder, tear-out gated on capability.tearOut with the gesture absent rather than broken where it is false, re-dock by adoption, the empty-window rule, duplicate tabs with DVTab(route, duplicate: true), deduplication by route -- which was by object identity and only worked because const canonicalisation made two literal tabs the same object -- and persistence through persistWorkspace/restoreWorkspace with unresolvable routes dropped. Persistence is scoped: the stored layout is keyed by tenant and user as well as the workspace name, so one person's open tabs are not the next person's at the same desk nor the same person's in another tenant. The switcher is built: on a TV the strip is a row of tiles the D-pad moves between and select chooses, on a watch a stack to tap, and on both moving or closing a tab is an action on the tab's menu rather than a drag; the presentation follows the device and a page can name it. Absent: same-engine hit-testing across windows, so re-dock between two real windows is adoption rather than an object handover.

Nothing this section asks for is unbuilt; what is not free is Pro, in dartvel_studio_pro in the private enterprise repository, attached through DVStudioSection and the editor's hook and publisher seams so an open-source build has no tab that opens onto nothing. Free: five leaf node types (text, image, button, spacer, divider), the layout boxes, the inspector, undo and redo, publish and revert, code export. Approval before a page goes live is Pro: an editor's Publish submits, an approver's decision writes the page, both audited. Multi-user editing is Pro: the free controller publishes every mutation as a DVStudioEdit and applies one from elsewhere, and dartvel_studio_pro carries them between sessions over a transport with the page's presence channel, viewer/editor roles and an audit trail. Revision history beyond in-session undo is Pro the same way: dartvel_studio_pro keeps a numbered, timestamped, attributed copy of a page at every save and restores any of them from a History tab. Reusable components are Pro the same way: dartvel_studio_pro's Components tab saves any page node as a named template, places instances with fresh ids, and pushes a change to every instance across every stored page. Responsive breakpoints are built: a node carries mobile-first per-breakpoint overrides, the renderer resolves them against context.screen.breakpoint, and the export switches on the breakpoint rather than flattening to one width. The visual backend workflow builder is not absent but Pro: it moved to dartvel_studio_pro in the private enterprise repository and attaches through DVStudioSection, so an open-source build has no Workflows tab. A Figma import -- every top-level frame of a file becomes a DVPageDocument, editable in the builder and exportable as an ordinary @DVPage -- also lives in dartvel_studio_pro, attached the same way, with the frames' auto-layout, fills, text styles and image fills mapped onto the node properties the renderer already paints

Nothing named. The dartvel inspect family is registered and runs against a real project: verified by running inspect, inspect routes, inspect models, inspect functions and inspect jobs on the site, not by reading the command table

Nothing named. Resumable imports chunk against a shared tested chunker that reads the header once, skips it as a row and attaches it to every chunk -- without which a worker handed chunk 2 of a CSV had no column order and resumable CSV import could not work at all. Scheduled reports parse their cron where the schedule is declared, so an unusable one fails there rather than silently never running

The Android Keystore row; there the key falls back to a file only the user can read, and DVAppKeyStores.describe says so rather than implying keyring protection. Built on the web, in Chrome: a non-extractable WebCrypto key in IndexedDB seals the application key at rest, the sealed bytes being what IndexedDB holds. Built and exercised on their own runners: the Windows row -- the key sealed with DPAPI to this user on this machine, the sealed blob being what sits on disk -- and the macOS row, a generic-password item in the Keychain through the Security framework; and the Linux row -- the Secret Service through libsecret, keyring-backed, exercised in CI on a private session bus with an unlocked GNOME keyring rather than skipped -- the 0600 file store it falls back to, the chooser that picks on what answers, and `dartvel key generate|rotate|status`, which refuses to replace a key that exists, rotates deliberately recording both fingerprints, and never prints the key. Also built: rotation hooks (DV.Secrets.onRotate fires when a resolver reports a new value, every hook runs even if one throws, the same value fires nothing) and DV.Test.withSecrets, which restores values and hooks after a test, on a throw too. The declaration manifest and DV-SECRETS-001 are built: dartvel build parses dartvel.secrets, refuses a client-scoped secret without the PUBLIC_ prefix, and fails with the file and the remedy when a backend-scoped secret is reached from client code. dvValidateEnvironment answers what deploy needs to check

Calling the clouds themselves, which needs credentials rather than code. dartvel deploy --functions writes a deployment artifact per backend function for lambda, cloud-run, container, edge, fly, railway and bare-metal, and refuses to ship an environment whose declared required secrets do not resolve

Nothing named. DV.$, dartvel sh and dartvel task all work, the last reading tasks from dartvel.tasks in pubspec.yaml -- verified by declaring one and running it, which is how the shell was found to be discarding the output of any command that exited quickly

Built: the runtime registry -- DV.Modules with its ids, lookup that names the registered ones when an id is unknown, a read-only lifecycle signal per module, and paths resolved against the mount point -- and mounting at build time. The build reads dartvel.modules, finds each module's project, takes the module's own route base off and puts the mount point on (the standalone /products/:id is /store/products/:id mounted), and the parent's router serves the module's own generated page at that path; the routes are in the parent's route manifest tagged with the module they came from, which is what the sitemap, the route explorer and the web server's manifest read. A mounted module is generated before the parent, since the parent imports its generated client, and one mounted twice is generated once. modules.g.dart registers every mount and gives each a typed accessor, so DV.Modules.notes is the module the build mounted. A backend-only module contributes no pages; a bad mount or a missing source is a reported problem rather than a crash. The example application mounts a real module, so every runtime job compiles a mounted module's routes and registry. Absent: every deployment mode past embedded -- split-backend deploys the module's backend as its own service with generated clients, and federated builds it independently and verifies a signed manifest before integration, neither of which is built; a backend-only module's models, functions and jobs are not merged into the parent; the shell, auth, theme and data modes; the export/inherit declarations for globals (the scoped registries themselves are built: DV.Modules.<id>.global<T>() is the module's own, and reading one never registered fails naming the module it looked in); and the capability check that refuses a mount a target cannot satisfy. Built since: a module's assets are the paths that find them in the parent -- Flutter serves another package's files under packages/<name>/, so DV.Modules.<id>.asset() answers with the mounted path and a path the module never declared comes back as itself rather than as a guess -- and its pages are typed targets, named for the route inside the module rather than for the mount, so the same module mounted elsewhere keeps the names and moves the paths. The example application mounts a module with a real asset, and CI checks that the module's screen renders at its route in a browser and that its asset is in the bundle under its package path.

nothing. `dartvel build web` writes a page per route, expands parameterised routes through the application's own resolvers, and gives each page its head tags, structured data and crawler-visible HTML. A model provider needs its data source reachable at build time, which is how static generation works everywhere; a provider that cannot resolve is named and skipped rather than ending the build

The pipeline the section describes is built, and it is one pipeline in dartvel_core that every server renders through: route resolved against the manifest's patterns with its parameters, page data resolved by the declared mode (awaited; cached for a ttl; served stale and refreshed behind the response; deferred to the client), visibility checked (hidden is 404, unauthorized 401, each the shell without the data), the head generated from the data (title, description, image made absolute against the site, canonical), structured data written as JSON-LD, the page's favicon selected, the crawler-visible text generated from the data, the Flutter bootstrap kept, and, with streaming on, the head sent as its own chunk. The resolver is generated: model_pages.g.dart, pure Dart beside the models, names where each public model page's rows are and which fields carry its title, content, image and published flag, and the generated backend builds the route's resolver from it over the application's database and starts its server with it -- so with spaRoot the built site's /users/ada is Ada's page when it is asked for, hidden when unpublished or absent. dartvel.web.server (pageDataMode, cacheTtlSeconds, streaming, cache) travels in the manifest. The kept pages can be shared: given any DVCacheAdapter -- Redis where the deployment has one -- they go there as JSON with when they were kept, so a second instance serves what the first resolved rather than resolving every page for itself, and the manifest's ttl is honoured (the backend's fallback built its cache before reading the manifest, so a declared five minutes lasted sixty seconds). A page is fresh for the ttl and servable stale for the stale window after it, both declarable; a lifetime of nothing is not written, which is what Redis says when it refuses an expire time of zero. Proven against a real Redis in CI: two connections, one cache, one resolve. Structured data is typed per model: @DVModel(schemaType: 'Product') travels into the generated page spec and becomes the page's JSON-LD @type, and a model that declares none is a Thing rather than a guess from the class's name. Absent: rendering Flutter widgets to HTML, which the section does not ask for.
